options.a: Reduced bank reserves and upward pressure on short-term interest rates
options.b: Higher reserve requirements that restrict new bank lending
options.c: An immediate cut in federal income tax rates by Congress
options.d: Increased bank reserves and downward pressure on short-term rates

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses open-market purchases with open-market sales; sales drain reserves and push short-term rates up.
distractorExplanations.b: Reserve requirements are a separate Fed tool; buying Treasuries changes reserve balances, not the required ratio.
distractorExplanations.c: Tax-rate cuts are fiscal policy enacted by Congress, not a result of Federal Reserve open-market operations.

options.a: Lower than short-term yields
options.b: Higher than short-term yields
options.c: Equal to short-term yields across maturities
options.d: Set directly by the Fed's discount rate

distractorExplanations.c: Equal yields across maturities describe a flat yield curve, not the normal upward-sloping shape.
distractorExplanations.d: The Fed's administered rates anchor the short end; long-term yields are market-set by inflation expectations and term premium.
distractorExplanations.a: That describes inversion.

options.a: Strong growth with rising inflation
options.b: Stagnant growth with high inflation
options.c: Falling growth with falling prices
options.d: High unemployment with stable prices

distractorExplanations.a: Strong growth with rising inflation describes an overheating late-cycle expansion, not stagnant growth.
distractorExplanations.c: Falling output with falling prices describes a deflationary recession; stagflation has rising prices.
distractorExplanations.d: High unemployment with stable prices is an ordinary recession; it lacks the elevated inflation of stagflation.

series-65-readiness-check-economics-005.explanation: Stagflation combines weak growth with elevated inflation. It often comes with high unemployment as well.

options.a: Firm-specific risk that a broad portfolio can reduce
options.b: Default risk on a single issuer's bonds
options.c: Market-wide risk that diversification cannot remove
options.d: Sector risk that spreading across industries removes

distractorExplanations.a: Describes unsystematic (idiosyncratic) risk, which diversification does reduce; systematic risk is market-wide.
distractorExplanations.b: Single-issuer credit risk is company-specific (unsystematic) risk that can be diversified, not market-wide risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Industry or sector risk is diversifiable unsystematic risk; systematic risk persists across every industry.

options.a: Moved about 20% less than the market on average
options.b: Moved about 20% more than the market on average
options.c: Returned 1.2% more than the market each year
options.d: Had 20% total volatility (standard deviation)

distractorExplanations.a: Moving about 20% less than the market describes a beta near 0.8; a beta above 1 means more movement.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses beta with alpha; beta measures sensitivity to market moves, not excess annual return.
distractorExplanations.d: Standard deviation measures total risk; beta measures relative systematic sensitivity versus the market.

options.a: Reserve requirements and the discount rate
options.b: Open-market operations by the Fed
options.c: Interest on reserve balances
options.d: Government spending and taxation

distractorExplanations.a: Reserve requirements and the discount rate are Federal Reserve monetary tools, not fiscal tools of Congress.
distractorExplanations.b: Open-market operations are the Fed's main monetary policy tool; fiscal policy is government taxing and spending.
distractorExplanations.c: Interest on reserve balances is an administered Fed rate, a monetary tool rather than a fiscal one.

options.a: Price changes received by domestic producers for output
options.b: Price changes for a basket of consumer goods/services
options.c: Total value of goods and services produced domestically
options.d: Price changes across everything included in GDP

distractorExplanations.a: That describes the Producer Price Index (PPI), which tracks prices producers receive, not consumer prices.
distractorExplanations.c: That is GDP, a measure of total output, not an index of consumer price changes.
distractorExplanations.d: That is the GDP price deflator, which covers all domestic output rather than a fixed consumer basket.

options.a: A sign of accelerating economic expansion
options.b: A possible recession warning signal
options.c: A signal that inflation is about to surge
options.d: Evidence that the Fed is cutting short rates

distractorExplanations.a: A steepening curve tends to accompany expansion; inversion has historically preceded recessions.
distractorExplanations.c: Inversion usually reflects expectations of lower future rates and inflation, not an imminent inflation surge.
distractorExplanations.d: Inversion typically occurs after the Fed has raised short rates above long yields, not while it is cutting.

options.a: The total explicit cash outlay for a choice
options.b: Costs already incurred that cannot be recovered
options.c: The extra cost of producing one more unit
options.d: The value of the next-best alternative forgone

distractorExplanations.a: Explicit outlays are accounting costs; opportunity cost is the implicit value of the best alternative given up.
distractorExplanations.b: Those are sunk costs, which should be ignored in decisions; opportunity cost looks forward at forgone options.
distractorExplanations.c: That is marginal cost, the cost of one more unit, not the value of the next-best alternative forgone.

options.a: GDP declines for two consecutive quarters
options.b: Unemployment rises while output stays flat
options.c: Unemployment falls and production rises
options.d: Prices fall as inventories pile up

distractorExplanations.a: Two straight quarters of falling GDP is the rule-of-thumb for contraction, the opposite of expansion.
distractorExplanations.b: Rising unemployment with flat output describes the contraction or trough phase, not expansion.
distractorExplanations.d: Falling prices and inventory build-ups characterize contraction, when demand weakens, not expansion.

options.a: Rising interest rates lowering bond prices
options.b: A single company's product recall
options.c: Unexpected inflation eroding real returns
options.d: Currency moves reducing foreign returns

distractorExplanations.a: That is interest-rate (market) risk; purchasing power risk is inflation eroding real returns.
distractorExplanations.d: That is exchange-rate (currency) risk on foreign holdings, not inflation eroding purchasing power.
distractorExplanations.b: Business-specific.

options.a: Are priced once daily at the closing NAV
options.b: Trade intraday on exchanges at market prices
options.c: Charge front-end sales loads on each purchase
options.d: Have a fixed share count like closed-end funds

distractorExplanations.a: Once-daily pricing at NAV describes open-end mutual funds; ETFs trade intraday at market prices.
distractorExplanations.c: ETF buyers pay brokerage commissions and spreads, not mutual-fund style front-end sales loads.
distractorExplanations.d: ETF shares are created and redeemed by authorized participants, so the share count is not fixed.

options.a: Inflation eroding purchasing power
options.b: Credit default by the U.S. Treasury
options.c: Rising rates lowering bond prices
options.d: Reinvestment risk on coupon payments

distractorExplanations.b: TIPS are Treasury obligations; their design feature is the CPI principal adjustment, not default protection.
distractorExplanations.c: TIPS still lose value when real yields rise; the inflation adjustment does not remove interest-rate risk.
distractorExplanations.d: TIPS pay semiannual coupons that must be reinvested, so they do not remove reinvestment risk.

options.a: Buy the stock at the strike only on expiration day
options.b: Sell the stock at the strike before expiration
options.c: Collect the premium if the option expires unexercised
options.d: Buy the stock at the strike before expiration

distractorExplanations.a: Exercise only at expiration is European style; American-style options can be exercised any time before expiry.
distractorExplanations.b: The right to sell at the strike belongs to a put buyer, not a call buyer.
distractorExplanations.c: The call writer keeps the premium when the option expires; the buyer pays the premium.

options.a: Higher credit risk and higher yields
options.b: Lower credit risk and usually higher yields
options.c: Lower credit risk and usually lower yields
options.d: Higher credit risk but lower interest-rate risk

distractorExplanations.b: Lower credit risk means investors accept smaller yield spreads, so investment-grade yields are usually lower.
distractorExplanations.d: Investment-grade bonds carry lower credit risk, and interest-rate risk depends on duration, not rating.
distractorExplanations.a: Opposite of IG vs HY.

options.a: Accretion/purchase discount to face value
options.b: Semiannual coupon payments reinvested
options.c: Price appreciation as interest rates rise
options.d: A premium paid back above par at maturity

distractorExplanations.b: Zero-coupon bonds pay no periodic coupons; return comes from accretion of the discount to par.
distractorExplanations.c: Bond prices fall when rates rise, and long-duration zeros fall the most.
distractorExplanations.d: Zeros are bought at a discount and mature at par, not at a premium above face value.

options.a: Direct ownership of a specific property deed
options.b: Limited partnership interests in oil pipelines
options.c: Tax-exempt revenue bonds funding housing projects
options.d: Real estate cash flows via a pooled security

distractorExplanations.a: REIT investors own shares of a pooled trust, not title to an individual property.
distractorExplanations.b: Pipeline partnership units describe MLPs (energy infrastructure), not real estate investment trusts.
distractorExplanations.c: Municipal housing bonds are tax-exempt debt; REIT dividends are generally taxable equity income.

options.a: Has priority over common for dividends but usually limited/no voting
options.b: Ranks ahead of bonds in liquidation but carries full voting rights
options.c: Has priority over common for dividends and grants extra votes per share
options.d: Pays a variable dividend that rises with earnings like common stock

distractorExplanations.b: Preferred ranks behind bondholders in liquidation and usually has limited or no voting rights.
distractorExplanations.c: Preferred does get dividend priority, but it usually has limited voting, not extra votes per share.
distractorExplanations.d: Preferred dividends are typically fixed; earnings-linked variable payouts are a common-stock trait.

options.a: Short-term, high-quality debt instruments
options.b: Long-term, high-quality government bonds
options.c: Short-term, below-investment-grade corporate debt
options.d: Listed preferred shares with stable dividends

distractorExplanations.b: Money market instruments mature in about a year or less; long-term government bonds are capital-market debt.
distractorExplanations.c: Money market instruments require high credit quality; short-term junk debt does not qualify.
distractorExplanations.d: Preferred stock is equity with no maturity, so it is not a short-term money market instrument.

options.a: Interest often exempt from federal income tax (and sometimes state)
options.b: Capital gains on sale exempt from federal income tax as well
options.c: Interest exempt from state income tax in any state of residence
options.d: Interest deductible against ordinary income on the investor's return

distractorExplanations.b: Only muni interest is typically federally exempt; capital gains on selling munis are taxable.
distractorExplanations.c: State exemption usually applies only to bonds issued in the investor's own state, not any state.
distractorExplanations.d: Muni interest is excluded from taxable income; it is not a deduction against other ordinary income.

options.a: The time remaining until a bond's final maturity
options.b: Bond price sensitivity to interest-rate changes
options.c: A bond's default probability over its life
options.d: Stock price sensitivity to market movements

distractorExplanations.a: That is term to maturity; duration is shorter for coupon bonds and measures rate sensitivity.
distractorExplanations.c: Default probability is credit risk, assessed through ratings and spreads, not duration.
distractorExplanations.d: Sensitivity of a stock to the market is beta; duration applies to bond price sensitivity to rates.

options.a: A foreign-currency bond issued by a U.S. corporation
options.b: A U.S. depositary receipt for a foreign company's shares
options.c: A dollar-denominated bond issued in the U.S. by a foreign firm
options.d: A U.S. dollar deposit held at a foreign bank

distractorExplanations.a: That is a foreign-currency denominated corporate bond, not a receipt representing foreign shares.
distractorExplanations.c: A dollar bond sold in the U.S. by a foreign issuer is a Yankee bond, debt rather than a share receipt.
distractorExplanations.d: Dollar deposits at foreign banks are Eurodollars, not depositary receipts for foreign equity.

options.a: The issuer calling when rates fall, forcing reinvestment at lower yields
options.b: The issuer calling when rates rise, forcing reinvestment at higher yields
options.c: Mandatory conversion into common shares when the stock price falls
options.d: Unlimited price appreciation as rates fall, unlike noncallable bonds

distractorExplanations.b: Issuers call bonds when rates fall to refinance cheaply; rising rates make a call unlikely.
distractorExplanations.c: Conversion features belong to convertible bonds; a call returns cash at the call price.
distractorExplanations.d: Callable bonds suffer price compression near the call price as rates fall, so upside is limited.

options.a: Daily redemption at NAV and registration under the Investment Company Act
options.b: Lower fees, daily liquidity, and open availability to any retail investor
options.c: Restrictions on short selling and leverage under the 1940 Act's diversification rules
options.d: More flexible strategies, higher fees, and often accredited-investor eligibility

distractorExplanations.a: Daily redeemability and 1940 Act registration describe mutual funds; hedge funds rely on exemptions.
distractorExplanations.b: These are mutual fund traits; hedge funds charge performance fees, restrict liquidity, and limit eligibility.
distractorExplanations.c: Leverage and shorting limits apply to registered funds; hedge funds commonly use both.

options.a: Balance risk/return across asset classes aligned to goals and risk tolerance
options.b: Pick the individual securities expected to outperform within each sector
options.c: Shift between stocks and cash based on short-term market forecasts
options.d: Maximize expected return by concentrating in the best-performing asset class

distractorExplanations.b: Choosing individual winners is security selection, a separate step from allocating among asset classes.
distractorExplanations.c: Forecast-driven switching is market timing, not the purpose of strategic asset allocation.
distractorExplanations.d: Concentrating in one class abandons diversification; allocation balances risk and return to goals.

options.a: A higher bond allocation than a retiree who needs portfolio income soon
options.b: A higher equity allocation than a retiree needing income soon
options.c: Heavy use of margin to boost equity exposure beyond 100%
options.d: A stable-value and money-market core to avoid volatility

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the logic; a long horizon and high tolerance support more equities, not more bonds.
distractorExplanations.c: High risk tolerance does not make leverage the default; margin adds risk beyond a suitable baseline.
distractorExplanations.d: A cash-like core suits short horizons; over decades it exposes a young investor to inflation erosion.

options.a: Roth IRAs during the original owner's lifetime
options.b: Taxable brokerage accounts once the account owner reaches age 73
options.c: Traditional IRAs/401(k)s after the applicable RMD age
options.d: 529 plans once the beneficiary reaches age 18

distractorExplanations.a: Roth IRAs have no RMDs while the original owner is alive; RMDs target pre-tax accounts.
distractorExplanations.b: RMDs apply to tax-deferred retirement accounts; taxable brokerage accounts have no required distributions.
distractorExplanations.d: 529 plans have no federal required distribution at 18; assets can stay invested for later education costs.

series-65-readiness-check-client-005.explanation: RMDs apply to most pre-tax retirement accounts starting at the statutory age. The applicable age has changed under the SECURE Acts, so rules evolve.

options.a: Specific securities to buy and target prices for each trade
options.b: A target return the adviser commits to achieving each year
options.c: Short-term market forecasts that drive monthly allocation shifts
options.d: Goals, constraints, risk tolerance, and allocation guidelines

distractorExplanations.a: An IPS sets policy and allocation guidelines, not trade-level security picks and price targets.
distractorExplanations.b: An IPS states return objectives, but no adviser can commit to achieving a return each year.
distractorExplanations.c: An IPS is a long-term policy document, not a vehicle for tactical short-term forecasts.

options.a: Growth stocks to build the down payment faster
options.b: Long-term bonds to lock in higher current yields
options.c: A balanced 60/40 portfolio to blend growth with steady income
options.d: Capital preservation and liquidity over high expected return

distractorExplanations.a: A 12-month goal cannot absorb an equity drawdown; growth stocks risk a shortfall when cash is needed.
distractorExplanations.b: Long-duration bonds can drop in price if rates rise before the 12-month need, risking principal.
distractorExplanations.c: A 60/40 mix suits long horizons; it still carries meaningful drawdown risk over a 12-month window.

options.a: Remove systematic risk by combining many assets across sectors
options.b: Reduce systematic risk by combining perfectly correlated assets
options.c: Raise expected return above the highest-returning asset held
options.d: Reduce unsystematic risk by combining imperfectly correlated assets

distractorExplanations.a: Systematic (market) risk remains however many assets are held; diversification reduces unsystematic risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Perfectly correlated assets give no diversification benefit, and it is unsystematic risk that falls.
distractorExplanations.c: A portfolio's expected return is a weighted average; diversification improves risk, not return beyond the best asset.

options.a: Marginal rates rise as taxable income rises
options.b: Everyone pays the same percentage of income
options.c: Lower earners pay a higher share of income
options.d: Tax rates rise as the holding period of assets lengthens

distractorExplanations.b: Paying the same percentage of income describes a flat (proportional) tax, not a progressive one.
distractorExplanations.c: A higher burden on lower earners describes a regressive tax, the opposite of progressive.
distractorExplanations.d: Holding period affects capital gains, and longer holding lowers the rate; progressivity is about income.

options.a: Buys more of the winners to ride recent momentum
options.b: Changes the target weights to match current market values
options.c: Moves the portfolio to cash until volatility subsides
options.d: Sells winners and buys laggards to restore target weights

distractorExplanations.a: Adding to winners is momentum investing, which lets weights drift further from targets.
distractorExplanations.b: Resetting targets to market values abandons the strategic allocation; rebalancing restores the targets.
distractorExplanations.c: Moving to cash on volatility is market timing, not restoring target weights.

options.a: Overestimate their ability to pick winning stocks
options.b: Anchor on the price they originally paid for a stock
options.c: Feel losses more strongly than equivalent gains
options.d: Follow the crowd into popular investments

distractorExplanations.a: Overestimating stock-picking skill is overconfidence bias, not loss aversion.
distractorExplanations.b: Fixating on the purchase price is anchoring bias, related to but distinct from loss aversion.
distractorExplanations.d: Following the crowd is herding bias; loss aversion is feeling losses more than equal gains.

options.a: Contain untrue statements of material fact or be misleading
options.b: Include performance results presented net of advisory fees
options.c: Describe the adviser's investment methods and their material risks
options.d: Include testimonials that carry the required disclosures

distractorExplanations.b: Net-of-fee performance is required under the marketing rule, not prohibited.
distractorExplanations.c: Accurately describing methods and their risks is permitted and supports a fair, balanced presentation.
distractorExplanations.d: The marketing rule permits testimonials when the required disclosures and oversight conditions are met.

series-65-readiness-check-ethics-001.explanation: Ads cannot be false or misleading; marketing rule sets detailed standards. Advertisements may not be otherwise misleading either.

options.a: The adviser through general overhead like office rent
options.b: Clients through research/brokerage services
options.c: The broker-dealer through higher order flow volume
options.d: Clients through lower commission rates on every trade

distractorExplanations.a: Office rent and general overhead are not research or brokerage services under the Section 28(e) safe harbor.
distractorExplanations.c: Soft dollars must benefit client accounts through research, not boost the executing broker's volume.
distractorExplanations.d: Soft-dollar deals usually involve paying more than execution-only rates; the client benefit is research.

options.a: SIPC coverage of advisory fees if the adviser fails
options.b: A requirement to register as a broker-dealer with FINRA
options.c: Additional Advisers Act custody rule requirements
options.d: Exemption from fiduciary duty for custodied accounts

distractorExplanations.a: SIPC protects customers of failed broker-dealers; it does not cover advisory fees or custody status.
distractorExplanations.b: Custody triggers custody rule duties for the adviser, not broker-dealer registration with FINRA.
distractorExplanations.d: Fiduciary duty applies to every advisory account; custody adds safeguards rather than removing duties.

series-65-readiness-check-ethics-003.explanation: Custody increases compliance obligations under Rule 206(4)-2 themes. Examples include a qualified custodian, client notices, and a surprise exam in many cases.

options.a: Trade allocation under a block order
options.b: Front-running / breach of duty
options.c: Interpositioning by a broker-dealer
options.d: Permissible agency cross transaction

distractorExplanations.a: Fair allocation of an aggregated block order is legitimate; trading ahead of clients is front-running.
distractorExplanations.c: Interpositioning inserts a third party between a customer and the best market; it is not trading ahead.
distractorExplanations.d: An agency cross means acting as broker for both sides with consent, not trading ahead of client orders.

options.a: Provides clients with material disclosures about fees and conflicts
options.b: Registers the adviser's representatives with state regulators
options.c: Serves as the client's written consent to principal trades
options.d: Satisfies the adviser's duty to determine client suitability

distractorExplanations.b: Representatives register through Form U4; ADV Part 2 is a client disclosure brochure.
distractorExplanations.c: Principal-trade consent must be obtained transaction by transaction; the brochure cannot supply it.
distractorExplanations.d: Disclosure does not replace the fiduciary duty to determine suitability and act in the client's best interest.

series-65-readiness-check-ethics-005.explanation: The brochure is a key client disclosure document. It also describes the advisory business and services.

options.a: Acceptable if gross returns are shown
options.b: Misleading cherry-picking
options.c: Allowed for institutional audiences
options.d: A valid composite presentation

distractorExplanations.a: Showing gross returns does not cure cherry-picking; selective account results remain misleading.
distractorExplanations.c: Audience sophistication does not make selective best-account performance a fair presentation.
distractorExplanations.d: A composite must include every similar account, not just the best performers, to be fair.

options.a: Registration of the solicitor as a broker-dealer with FINRA
options.b: Client consent before each solicitor payment is made
options.c: Required disclosures/agreements under applicable marketing rules
options.d: Verbal disclosure after the client has signed the contract

distractorExplanations.a: Paid solicitation for an adviser triggers marketing rule disclosures, not broker-dealer registration.
distractorExplanations.b: Disclosure is given at the time of the solicitation; client consent to each payment is not required.
distractorExplanations.d: Disclosures must be provided at the time of the solicitation, not after the client has already signed.

series-65-readiness-check-ethics-007.explanation: Paid solicitation typically needs documented disclosures and compliance. Applicable rules include the solicitor and marketing rules.

options.a: Material information after a company's public press release
options.b: Material nonpublic information in breach of a duty
options.c: Analyst mosaic conclusions from public data
options.d: Nonmaterial nonpublic details about a company

distractorExplanations.a: Once information is broadly disseminated, such as by press release, it is public and may be traded on.
distractorExplanations.c: Mosaic theory allows conclusions built from public and nonmaterial pieces; it is not insider trading.
distractorExplanations.d: Insider trading liability requires material information; nonmaterial details do not trigger it.

options.a: The most favorable total execution quality reasonably available
options.b: The fastest fill available at any trading venue
options.c: The lowest advertised commission only, ignoring quality
options.d: The broker that provides the most soft-dollar research to the adviser

distractorExplanations.b: Speed is one factor; best execution weighs price, costs, research value, and reliability together.
distractorExplanations.d: Soft-dollar research cannot override best execution; execution quality must still be evaluated.
distractorExplanations.c: Too narrow.

series-65-readiness-check-ethics-009.explanation: Best execution is about overall quality, not solely sticker commission. The standard is applied under the circumstances of each trade.

options.a: A blanket consent in the advisory contract signed at account opening
options.b: Disclosure and client consent as required under Advisers Act rules
options.c: Disclosure only in Form ADV Part 2 without separate client approval
options.d: Approval by the adviser's chief compliance officer instead of the client

distractorExplanations.a: Section 206(3) requires disclosure and consent for each principal trade; blanket contract consent is insufficient.
distractorExplanations.c: Brochure disclosure alone does not satisfy the transaction-specific client consent required for principal trades.
distractorExplanations.d: Internal compliance approval cannot substitute for the client's own consent to a principal trade.

options.a: Remain prohibited for SEC-registered advisers
options.b: May be used without disclosure if unpaid
options.c: May be used if conditions/disclosures are met
options.d: Require prior approval by SEC staff before use

distractorExplanations.a: The modern marketing rule replaced the old testimonial ban; testimonials are allowed with conditions.
distractorExplanations.b: Even unpaid testimonials need disclosures, such as whether the person is a client and any conflicts.
distractorExplanations.d: The SEC does not pre-approve testimonials; the adviser must meet the rule's conditions and oversight.

options.a: Disclosed only if the client asks about it directly
options.b: Identified, disclosed, and mitigated/eliminated as appropriate
options.c: Disclosed once at onboarding and then left unmanaged
options.d: Reported to the SEC instead of being disclosed to clients

distractorExplanations.a: The fiduciary duty is proactive; material conflicts must be disclosed without waiting for a client question.
distractorExplanations.c: Conflict management is ongoing; a single disclosure with no mitigation or updates is insufficient.
distractorExplanations.d: The duty runs to clients; a regulatory filing does not replace disclosure to the affected clients.

options.a: Kept for one year and then destroyed by policy
options.b: Kept only for clients with discretionary accounts
options.c: Kept for required periods and available for inspection
options.d: Filed with the SEC each quarter in place of retention

distractorExplanations.a: Advisers must generally keep records five years, the first two in an appropriate office, not one year.
distractorExplanations.b: Recordkeeping duties cover every advisory client, not just discretionary accounts.
distractorExplanations.d: Records are retained by the adviser and produced on inspection; quarterly SEC filing does not replace retention.

options.a: A single quarter of negative real GDP growth
options.b: A 20% decline in a broad stock market index from its peak
options.c: A sustained rise in the general price level across the economy
options.d: A significant decline in economic activity spread across the economy

distractorExplanations.a: One weak quarter is not enough; recessions involve broad, sustained declines across the economy.
distractorExplanations.b: A 20% index decline from the peak is the common bear market definition, not a recession.
distractorExplanations.c: A sustained rise in the general price level is inflation, not a decline in economic activity.

options.a: Lower consumer spending as households save more
options.b: Immediate Fed rate cuts to support demand
options.c: Higher consumer spending and near-term growth
options.d: Lower bond yields as investors seek safety

distractorExplanations.a: Rising confidence usually lowers precautionary saving and raises spending, not the reverse.
distractorExplanations.b: Stronger confidence boosts demand on its own; it does not call for Fed rate cuts to support demand.
distractorExplanations.d: Optimism tends to push yields up as investors move away from safe assets, not toward them.

options.a: Demand-side stimulus from lower energy bills
options.b: Demand-pull inflation driven by excess spending
options.c: Monetary policy tightening by the Federal Reserve
options.d: Supply-side shock that can raise production costs

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses cost-push with demand-pull; an oil price spike raises costs from the supply side.
distractorExplanations.c: Oil prices are set in commodity markets; Fed tightening is a policy action, not a supply shock.
distractorExplanations.a: Higher oil prices raise costs; they do not cut bills.

options.a: How frequently money changes hands in the economy
options.b: The rate at which the Fed expands the money supply
options.c: The share of income households save each year
options.d: How quickly bank deposits multiply through lending

distractorExplanations.b: Money supply growth is the M in MV=PY; velocity is how often each dollar is spent.
distractorExplanations.c: The share of income saved is the personal saving rate, not the velocity of money.
distractorExplanations.d: Deposit expansion through lending is the money multiplier, a different concept from velocity.

options.a: Make U.S. exports more competitive abroad
options.b: Make imported goods cheaper for U.S. buyers
options.c: Raise the dollar value of foreign investment returns
options.d: Make foreign travel more expensive for Americans

distractorExplanations.c: A stronger dollar reduces the dollar value of foreign-currency returns for U.S. investors.
distractorExplanations.d: A stronger dollar buys more foreign currency, making foreign travel cheaper for Americans.
distractorExplanations.a: Stronger dollar usually makes exports relatively expensive.

options.a: Higher tax revenue pushes down interest rates and increases private business investment
options.b: Government spending raises private incomes and multiplies total output
options.c: Higher government borrowing pushes up interest rates and reduces private investment
options.d: Fed bond purchases push down interest rates and boost private borrowing

distractorExplanations.a: That describes crowding in from reduced government borrowing, the opposite of crowding out.
distractorExplanations.b: That is the fiscal multiplier effect, not the rate-driven reduction in private investment.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes monetary easing such as quantitative easing, not fiscal crowding out.

options.a: Frictional and cyclical unemployment at full employment
options.b: Cyclical unemployment caused by recession layoffs
options.c: Workers who have stopped looking for work
options.d: Frictional and structural unemployment at full employment

distractorExplanations.a: Cyclical unemployment is near zero at the natural rate; it is frictional plus structural.
distractorExplanations.b: Recession layoffs are cyclical unemployment, which is excluded from the natural rate.
distractorExplanations.c: Discouraged workers are outside the labor force and are not counted in the unemployment rate.

options.a: Hold a larger fraction of deposits as reserves, reducing funds available to lend
options.b: Hold a smaller fraction of deposits as reserves, increasing funds available to lend
options.c: Raise the discount rate charged on overnight borrowing from the Fed
options.d: Hold more capital against loans under Basel risk-weighting standards

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the effect; a higher requirement ties up more deposits and reduces lending capacity.
distractorExplanations.c: The Fed sets the discount rate; member banks do not raise it in response to reserve requirements.
distractorExplanations.d: Capital requirements are a separate bank regulation; reserve requirements apply to deposits.

options.a: Priority over preferred stockholders for dividends
options.b: A fixed dividend set at issuance like preferred stock
options.c: A claim on assets ahead of unsecured bondholders
options.d: Voting rights and residual claim on assets after creditors

distractorExplanations.a: Preferred stockholders receive dividends before common stockholders, not after.
distractorExplanations.b: Common dividends are discretionary and variable; a fixed stated dividend is a preferred feature.
distractorExplanations.c: Common stockholders rank last, behind every class of creditor including unsecured bondholders.

options.a: Buy the underlying asset at the strike price before or at expiration
options.b: Receive the premium if the underlying stays above the strike
options.c: Sell the underlying at the strike price before or at expiration
options.d: Sell the underlying at the market price on expiration day

distractorExplanations.a: The right to buy at the strike describes a call option, not a put.
distractorExplanations.b: Keeping the premium when the price stays above the strike is the put writer's outcome, not the holder's.
distractorExplanations.d: A put locks in the strike price; selling at the market price needs no option.

options.a: Redeem shares daily at NAV with the fund company
options.b: Continuously issue new shares as investors buy in
options.c: Trade on exchanges at prices fixed to their NAV
options.d: Trade on exchanges at prices that can differ from NAV

distractorExplanations.b: Continuous issuance of new shares is an open-end fund feature; closed-end funds have a fixed share count.
distractorExplanations.c: Closed-end market prices float and often sit at a premium or discount to NAV.
distractorExplanations.a: Open-end funds redeem at NAV; closed-end funds generally do not.

options.a: Exchange the bond for a predetermined number of shares
options.b: Exchange the bond for cash at par before maturity
options.c: Receive a coupon that resets with a benchmark rate
options.d: Buy additional shares at a set price via attached warrants

distractorExplanations.b: Redeeming for cash at par before maturity is a put feature of putable bonds, not conversion.
distractorExplanations.c: A coupon that resets with a benchmark describes a floating-rate note, not a convertible.
distractorExplanations.d: Warrants are separate purchase rights; a convertible exchanges the bond itself for shares.

options.a: Investment-grade ratings and higher yield spreads
options.b: Non-investment-grade ratings and lower yield spreads
options.c: Non-investment-grade ratings and higher yield spreads
options.d: Ratings of BBB or above with low default rates

distractorExplanations.a: Junk bonds are below investment grade; investment-grade issuers pay narrower spreads.
distractorExplanations.b: Investors demand wider, not narrower, yield spreads to hold non-investment-grade credit.
distractorExplanations.d: BBB-/Baa3 and above is investment grade; junk bonds are rated BB+/Ba1 or lower.

options.a: Commercial real estate such as office towers
options.b: Technology and biotech venture investments
options.c: Municipal water and transit infrastructure
options.d: Energy and natural-resource infrastructure

distractorExplanations.a: Commercial real estate ownership is the domain of REITs, not master limited partnerships.
distractorExplanations.b: MLPs must earn qualifying income, largely from natural resources, not venture technology investments.
distractorExplanations.c: Municipal water and transit projects are financed by muni bonds, not structured as MLPs.

series-65-readiness-check-products-024.explanation: MLPs often own pipelines and pass income to unit holders with unique tax reporting. MLPs use pass-through taxation, so unit holders receive Schedule K-1s.

options.a: Issuer credit risk plus embedded derivative payoff formulas
options.b: FDIC insurance on principal up to $250,000 per depositor
options.c: Principal protection backed by the U.S. Treasury
options.d: SIPC coverage against the issuer's default

distractorExplanations.b: Structured notes are unsecured issuer debt; FDIC insurance covers bank deposits, not these notes.
distractorExplanations.c: Any principal protection depends on the issuer's credit, not on U.S. Treasury backing.
distractorExplanations.d: SIPC covers missing customer assets at a failed broker-dealer, not losses from issuer default.

options.a: Tax-free growth and withdrawals after age 59½
options.b: Tax-deferred growth and insurer-guaranteed minimum interest
options.c: Tax-deferred growth and returns tied to subaccount performance
options.d: SIPC protection on cash value like a brokerage account

distractorExplanations.a: Tax-free qualified withdrawals describe a Roth IRA; annuity gains are taxed as ordinary income.
distractorExplanations.c: Returns tied to subaccounts describe a variable annuity, not a fixed annuity.
distractorExplanations.d: SIPC covers broker-dealer failures; fixed annuity guarantees depend on the insurer's claims-paying ability.

series-65-readiness-check-products-026.explanation: Fixed annuities are insurance products with contractual guarantees subject to insurer strength. Payout terms are set per contract.

options.a: Selling call options to generate premium income while capping upside
options.b: Buying put options to protect against a decline in the stock
options.c: Selling put options to collect premium and possibly buy more of the shares
options.d: Writing calls without owning the stock to collect premium income

distractorExplanations.b: Buying puts against owned stock is a protective put, a hedge, not a covered call.
distractorExplanations.c: Selling puts to possibly acquire shares is a cash-secured put strategy, not a covered call.
distractorExplanations.d: Writing calls without the stock is a naked (uncovered) call with unlimited risk.

options.a: Increase the longer shares are held before redemption
options.b: Decline over time and may apply on redemptions within a stated period
options.c: Are deducted from each purchase as a front-end load
options.d: Are annual 12b-1 fees charged for distribution and marketing costs

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the schedule; CDSC percentages decline the longer shares are held.
distractorExplanations.c: Charges deducted at purchase are front-end loads (Class A), not contingent deferred charges.
distractorExplanations.d: 12b-1 fees are ongoing annual distribution fees, separate from a back-end CDSC on redemption.

options.a: Recent trade history and preferred securities to buy
options.b: Return targets the adviser commits to deliver each year
options.c: The adviser's own model portfolio performance history
options.d: Goals, time horizon, financial situation, and risk tolerance

distractorExplanations.a: Trade history and preferences alone miss the client's goals, horizon, and capacity for risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Advisers cannot commit to deliver returns; profiling records the client's goals and constraints.
distractorExplanations.c: The firm's model performance does not describe the client's needs, finances, or risk tolerance.

options.a: How quickly assets must be available as cash without major loss
options.b: How much of the portfolio is invested in exchange-listed securities
options.c: How much long-term appreciation the client needs to meet goals
options.d: How much volatility the client can tolerate without selling

distractorExplanations.b: Exchange listing affects marketability; liquidity need is when the client requires cash.
distractorExplanations.c: Needed appreciation is the return objective, separate from how quickly cash must be available.
distractorExplanations.d: Comfort with volatility is risk tolerance, not the client's need for accessible cash.

options.a: The period over which the adviser expects to outperform a benchmark
options.b: The expected period before the client needs to use the invested funds
options.c: The average holding period of each security in the portfolio
options.d: The years remaining before the client's bond holdings mature

distractorExplanations.a: Outperformance expectations concern the manager, not when the client will need the money.
distractorExplanations.c: Average holding period is a turnover measure, not the client's planning horizon.
distractorExplanations.d: Bond maturities are portfolio traits that should be matched to the horizon, not define it.

options.a: Emotional willingness to accept portfolio volatility
options.b: The client's stated preference for growth over income
options.c: Financial ability to absorb losses without derailing goals
options.d: The maximum return the client hopes to earn each year

distractorExplanations.a: Emotional willingness to accept volatility is risk tolerance, the subjective side, not capacity.
distractorExplanations.b: A preference for growth is an investment objective, not an objective measure of loss capacity.
distractorExplanations.d: Hoped-for return is a return objective; capacity is the financial ability to absorb losses.

options.a: A short horizon that calls for capital preservation and liquidity
options.b: A need for income-producing bonds to cover living expenses
options.c: Constraints similar to a retiree taking required distributions
options.d: A long horizon that may support higher equity allocation if suitable

distractorExplanations.a: A 30-year retirement goal is a long horizon; preservation and liquidity fit short horizons.
distractorExplanations.b: A working professional saving for retirement is accumulating, not drawing portfolio income for expenses.
distractorExplanations.c: Retirees face withdrawal, RMD, and sequence risk constraints that a young saver does not.

options.a: Selling securities at a loss to offset gains, subject to wash-sale rules
options.b: Selling appreciated securities to reset cost basis higher, subject to holding rules
options.c: Selling securities at a loss and rebuying them within 30 days to keep the deduction
options.d: Donating appreciated securities to charity to avoid capital gains

distractorExplanations.b: Realizing gains to step up basis is gain harvesting, not harvesting losses to offset gains.
distractorExplanations.c: Repurchasing substantially identical securities within 30 days triggers the wash-sale rule and disallows the loss.
distractorExplanations.d: Gifting appreciated securities is a charitable strategy, not selling losers to offset gains.

options.a: Holding an active state insurance producer license
options.b: Meeting income or net-worth thresholds defined in Regulation D
options.c: Having at least $250,000 in a single brokerage account
options.d: Having invested in at least three prior private placements

distractorExplanations.a: Insurance producer licenses do not confer accredited status; certain securities licenses such as Series 65 do.
distractorExplanations.c: Rule 501 uses $1 million net worth excluding the primary residence or income tests, not an account balance.
distractorExplanations.d: Past private placement experience is not one of the Regulation D accredited investor tests.

options.a: Selling the position at once to remove single-stock risk
options.b: Holding the position because past gains signal continued strength
options.c: Diversification, tax implications, and liquidity if the client sells
options.d: Adding margin to the position to amplify the expected upside

distractorExplanations.a: Immediate liquidation ignores tax consequences and the client's goals; options should be discussed first.
distractorExplanations.b: Past gains do not reduce concentration risk; this reflects recency and familiarity bias.
distractorExplanations.d: Margin on a concentrated position compounds single-stock risk rather than addressing it.

options.a: Drawing down Roth assets first so tax-deferred accounts grow longer
options.b: Withdrawing equally from each account type every year
options.c: Delaying all withdrawals until required distributions begin
options.d: Tax-efficient sourcing from taxable, tax-deferred, and tax-free accounts

distractorExplanations.a: Roth assets are usually tapped last; deferred accounts face RMDs and tax on withdrawal anyway.
distractorExplanations.b: Equal pro-rata withdrawals ignore bracket management and differing tax treatment across accounts.
distractorExplanations.c: Retirees need income before RMD age, and waiting can push later RMDs into higher brackets.

options.a: The client's holding period beyond one year, with longer periods taxed lower
options.b: The client's taxable income and filing status under current tax law
options.c: The type of security sold, with stocks taxed lower than bonds
options.d: The state where the brokerage firm is headquartered

distractorExplanations.a: Past one year every holding is long-term at the same rates; holding period only separates short from long.
distractorExplanations.c: Long-term gains on stocks and bonds use the same rate schedule; the brackets depend on income.
distractorExplanations.d: Federal rates depend on the client's income and filing status, not the broker's location.

options.a: Close the account immediately and transfer assets to heirs
options.b: Accept the client's instructions without any further review
options.c: Involve trusted contacts or legal guidance and document concerns
options.d: Take over decisions under the existing advisory agreement

distractorExplanations.a: An adviser has no authority to transfer assets to heirs; that requires legal authority or death.
distractorExplanations.b: Signs of diminished capacity call for heightened care, trusted-contact outreach, and documentation.
distractorExplanations.d: Investment discretion does not grant authority over a client's broader affairs; that needs a POA or court order.

series-65-readiness-check-client-027.explanation: Advisers should follow firm policy, document, and protect vulnerable clients within legal bounds. Concerns should be documented appropriately under firm policy.

options.a: Project a single expected return using historical averages
options.b: Measure a portfolio's sensitivity to interest-rate changes
options.c: Calculate the risk-adjusted return of past portfolio results
options.d: Model a range of outcomes using variable return assumptions

distractorExplanations.a: A single-return projection is a deterministic forecast; Monte Carlo models many possible paths.
distractorExplanations.b: Sensitivity to interest-rate changes is measured by duration, not Monte Carlo simulation.
distractorExplanations.c: Risk-adjusted past returns are measured by ratios like Sharpe; Monte Carlo models future outcomes.

options.a: Diversify investments unless the purpose of the account justifies concentration
options.b: Judge each investment on its own merits rather than as part of the overall portfolio
options.c: Avoid delegating investment functions to outside managers
options.d: Favor the highest-yielding investments to maximize current income

distractorExplanations.b: The prudent investor rule judges investments in the context of the whole portfolio, not in isolation.
distractorExplanations.c: The rule permits delegation, provided the fiduciary selects managers prudently and monitors them.
distractorExplanations.d: Chasing yield ignores the risk-return balance and diversification the prudent investor rule requires.

options.a: Converting the full IRA at once to minimize total taxes owed
options.b: Current and projected tax brackets, conversion amounts, and cash to pay taxes
options.c: Paying conversion taxes from the IRA to preserve taxable assets
options.d: Whether the client's modified AGI falls below the Roth conversion income limit

distractorExplanations.a: A single large conversion can push income into top brackets; partial conversions often reduce total tax.
distractorExplanations.c: Withholding tax from the IRA shrinks the amount converted and can add a penalty before age 59½.
distractorExplanations.d: The income limit on Roth conversions was eliminated in 2010; any IRA owner may convert.

options.a: Within 48 hours after the contract is signed, and then every two years thereafter
options.b: Before entering the contract, with updates delivered only upon client request
options.c: After the first trade settles in the account, and annually thereafter
options.d: Before or at the time of entering an advisory contract, and annually thereafter

distractorExplanations.a: Delivery is due before or at contract signing, and updates come annually, not every two years.
distractorExplanations.b: Annual delivery of a material-changes summary or updated brochure is required, not on request.
distractorExplanations.c: Delivery must occur before or at entering the advisory contract, not after the first trade settles.

options.a: Trade securities for personal or client benefit
options.b: Report the information to the firm's compliance department
options.c: Place the issuer on the firm's restricted or watch list
options.d: Inform legal counsel when assessing a disclosure obligation

distractorExplanations.b: Escalating MNPI to compliance is required by insider trading policies, not a prohibited use.
distractorExplanations.c: Restricting the issuer is a standard control that MNPI should prompt, not a prohibited use of it.
distractorExplanations.d: Sharing MNPI with counsel for legal advice is a legitimate use, not trading on the information.

series-65-readiness-check-ethics-017.explanation: Insider trading rules prohibit trading on MNPI. Trading on it before public disclosure is prohibited.

options.a: Annual holdings reports for clients' personal accounts
options.b: Personal trading reports and pre-clearance policies for access persons
options.c: Pre-clearance of all client trades by the chief compliance officer
options.d: Personal trading reports for every employee filed directly with the SEC

distractorExplanations.a: Code-of-ethics reports cover access persons' own holdings, not clients' personal accounts.
distractorExplanations.c: Pre-clearance applies to access persons' personal trades, such as IPOs and private placements, not client trades.
distractorExplanations.d: Access persons report to the adviser's CCO, not to the SEC, and not every employee is an access person.

options.a: Making political contributions of any amount to candidates in states where they have clients
options.b: Soliciting government clients through registered placement agents subject to pay-to-play rules
options.c: Providing advisory services for government entities after certain political contributions
options.d: Accepting compensation from private clients within two years of any campaign donation

distractorExplanations.a: The rule targets officials of government entity clients and allows de minimis $350/$150 contributions.
distractorExplanations.b: Paying regulated placement agents to solicit government entities is permitted; unregulated solicitors are barred.
distractorExplanations.d: The two-year time-out applies to compensation from government entity clients, not private clients.

options.a: Hold client securities in the adviser's own name at a qualified custodian
options.b: Send account statements to clients annually instead of the custodian quarterly
options.c: Undergo a surprise examination once every three years by the SEC staff
options.d: Use a qualified custodian and undergo an annual surprise examination if applicable

distractorExplanations.a: Accounts must be in the client's name or the adviser's name as agent or trustee, not the adviser's own name.
distractorExplanations.b: The qualified custodian must send account statements to clients at least quarterly.
distractorExplanations.c: The surprise exam is annual and performed by an independent public accountant, not SEC staff.

options.a: Material misstatements and omissions in advisory relationships
options.b: Charging performance fees to qualified clients under Rule 205-3
options.c: Agency cross transactions with written client consent
options.d: Recommending securities in which the adviser has a disclosed interest

distractorExplanations.b: Performance fees charged to qualified clients under Rule 205-3 are permitted, not fraudulent.
distractorExplanations.c: Agency cross trades with written consent and required disclosures are permitted under Rule 206(3)-2.
distractorExplanations.d: Recommending securities with a disclosed interest is allowed; the anti-fraud rules target nondisclosure.

options.a: May be shown to any retail audience as long as gross and net returns are presented together
options.b: Must include detailed assumptions and be distributed only to audiences who can evaluate it
options.c: Is permitted without further conditions as long as it is labeled hypothetical in a footnote
options.d: Must be pre-approved by SEC staff before any public distribution

distractorExplanations.a: Gross-and-net presentation applies to actual performance; hypotheticals also need audience-relevance policies.
distractorExplanations.c: A label is not enough; hypotheticals require assumptions, risk disclosures, and audience-targeting policies.
distractorExplanations.d: The SEC does not pre-approve advertisements; the adviser must meet the rule's conditions itself.

options.a: Holdings of each client account to every other client
options.b: Material conflicts only after a client raises a complaint
options.c: Soft-dollar benefits, referral arrangements, and any material conflicts
options.d: Its proprietary trading algorithms in full source-code detail to every client

distractorExplanations.a: Client holdings are confidential; disclosure duties concern the adviser's conflicts, not other clients' data.
distractorExplanations.b: Material conflicts must be disclosed proactively, not only after a client complains.
distractorExplanations.d: Advisers must describe methods and material risks, not hand over proprietary source code.

options.a: Repay the affected clients quietly from firm capital and close the matter without any report
options.b: Wait for the next annual compliance review to evaluate the issue
options.c: Terminate the employee and treat the matter as a personnel issue
options.d: Investigate, escalate per policy, and consider notifying regulators or law enforcement

distractorExplanations.a: Quiet repayment conceals misconduct and can breach reporting duties; the matter must be investigated and escalated.
distractorExplanations.b: Suspected theft requires prompt action; waiting for the annual review increases client harm.
distractorExplanations.c: Firing the employee does not address client losses, investigation, or possible reporting obligations.

series-65-readiness-check-ethics-024.explanation: Firms must address theft promptly and meet reporting obligations. Custodians may also need to be notified.

options.a: Services covered by the bundled fee and conflicts from bundling trading costs
options.b: Only the advisory portion of the fee, excluding brokerage services
options.c: Commissions charged on each trade executed within the wrap account
options.d: Each portfolio manager's personal securities holdings and recent trading history

distractorExplanations.b: The wrap brochure must describe the full bundled fee, including brokerage, and whether it may cost more.
distractorExplanations.c: A wrap fee replaces per-trade commissions; the brochure explains what the bundled fee covers.
distractorExplanations.d: Personal holdings of managers are code-of-ethics matters, not wrap fee brochure content.

options.a: Disclosure of the adviser's ranking among its peers for every year rated
options.b: Disclosure of the date and period of the rating and compensation ties if any
options.c: Approval from the rating agency's compliance team before each use
options.d: A statement that the SEC has reviewed the rating methodology

distractorExplanations.a: The rule does not require a year-by-year peer ranking; it requires date, period, provider, and compensation.
distractorExplanations.c: The marketing rule places conditions on the adviser; rating-agency approval of each use is not required.
distractorExplanations.d: Implying SEC review or endorsement of a rating is misleading; the SEC does not review ratings.

options.a: Voting with management on every ballot item to avoid conflicts
options.b: Voting every proxy, even when the cost exceeds the client benefit
options.c: Disclosure of how the adviser votes proxies and handles conflicts
options.d: Passing every vote decision to the client's custodian bank

distractorExplanations.a: Blanket management voting may not serve clients; votes must follow policies in clients' best interest.
distractorExplanations.b: SEC guidance lets advisers refrain from voting when the cost exceeds the expected client benefit.
distractorExplanations.d: Custodians forward ballots; an adviser with voting authority must vote under its own policies.

options.a: The adviser discloses the basis for the guarantee in Form ADV Part 2
options.b: A back-tested model supports the projected returns
options.c: The client signs a written risk acknowledgment first
options.d: No such guarantee may be made; performance is inherently uncertain

distractorExplanations.a: Disclosure cannot legitimize a promise of investment results; guaranteeing performance is prohibited.
distractorExplanations.b: Back-tested results are hypothetical and cannot support a guarantee of future performance.
distractorExplanations.c: A signed risk acknowledgment does not permit the adviser to guarantee investment results.

options.a: Written authorization and a custodian that sends statements to clients
options.b: Verbal authorization and a custodian that sends statements to the adviser
options.c: Written authorization and annual statements sent by the adviser itself
options.d: Client approval of each fee debit by phone before it is processed

distractorExplanations.b: Fee deduction needs written authorization, and custodian statements must go to clients, not the adviser.
distractorExplanations.c: The qualified custodian, not the adviser, must send statements, and at least quarterly.
distractorExplanations.d: A written authorization in the advisory agreement covers fee deduction; per-debit phone approval is not the rule.

series-65-readiness-check-ethics-029.explanation: Fee deduction from custodied accounts needs client consent and custodian oversight. Proper invoicing is also expected.

options.a: Allocate to the largest accounts first because they pay the most fees
options.b: Allocate fairly according to disclosed policy without favoritism
options.c: Allocate to performance-fee accounts first to maximize client returns
options.d: Allocate first to the adviser's proprietary accounts to test demand

distractorExplanations.a: Favoring fee-rich accounts is a conflict; allocations must follow a fair, disclosed policy.
distractorExplanations.c: Favoring performance-fee accounts benefits the adviser and violates fair allocation duties.
distractorExplanations.d: Placing proprietary accounts ahead of clients in scarce IPOs breaches the duty of loyalty.
